Reducing the frequency of milk recording and the number of recorded samples per test-day could be a solution in order to reduce costs of official milk recording. However, fewer samples lead to a decrease in the accuracy of predicted daily yields. Unfortunately, the current published equations use the milking interval that is often not available and/or reliable in practice. The first objective of this study was to propose models using easily available traits. Therefore the milking interval was replaced by a combination of data easily recorded by milk recording. The second objective of this study was to enlarge the previous investigations to milk fatty acids (FA) in order to propose a practical method for estimating accurate daily milk, fat and major FA yields from single milking. The fit goodness of proposed models was evaluated based on the correlation values between the estimated and observed daily yields in addition to the calculation of the mean square error. Obtained results are promising. Correlation values were comprised between 96.4% and 97.6% when daily yield were estimated from morning milking, and from 96.9% to 98.3% when daily yield were estimated from evening milking. The combination of records related to lactation stage, month of test, milk yield, and fat could replace the milking interval effect. Because of their simplicity, proposed models would be easy to implement.

data.Documented value: Predictions of Daily Milk and Fat Yields, Major Groups of Fatty Acids, and C18:1 cis-9 from Single Milking Data without a Milking Interval

Reducing the frequency of milk recording would help reduce the costs of official milk recording. However, this approach could also negatively affect the accuracy of predicting daily yields. This problem has been investigated in numerous studies. In addition, published equations take into account milking intervals (MI), and these are often not available and/or are unreliable in practice. The first objective of this study was to propose models in which the MI was replaced by a combination of data easily recorded by dairy farmers. The second objective was to further investigate the fatty acids (FA) present in milk. Equations to predict daily yield from AM or PM data were based on a calibration database containing 79,971 records related to 51 traits [milk yield (expected AM, expected PM, and expected daily); fat content (expected AM, expected PM, and expected daily); fat yield (expected AM, expected PM, and expected daily; g/day); levels of seven different FAs or FA groups (expected AM, expected PM, and expected daily; g/dL milk), and the corresponding FA yields for these seven FA types/groups (expected AM, expected PM, and expected daily; g/day)]. These equations were validated using two distinct external datasets. The results obtained from the proposed models were compared to previously published results for models which included a MI effect. The corresponding correlation values ranged from 96.4% to 97.6% when the daily yields were estimated from the AM milkings and ranged from 96.9% to 98.3% when the daily yields were estimated from the PM milkings. The simplicity of these proposed models should facilitate their use by breeding and milk recording organizations.

[[S2|Open Repository and Bibliography University of]] In the realm of dairy farming, the estimation of daily yield and the content of major fatty acids from a single milking is a crucial aspect. This section delves into the methodology and outcomes of a study aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of these estimations. [[S2|Open Repository and Bibliography University of]] The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Liège, aimed to develop models that could predict daily milk, fat, and major fatty acid yields from a single milking.

The primary objectives were to propose models using easily available traits and to expand previous investigations to include milk fatty acids (FA). The researchers replaced the milking interval with a combination of easily recorded traits, such as lactation stage, month of test, milk yield, and fat content, to enhance the accuracy of the predictions. [[S2|Open Repository and Bibliography University of]] The study evaluated the fit goodness of the proposed models based on the correlation values between the estimated and observed daily yields. The results were promising, with correlation values ranging from 96.4% to 98.3% when daily yields were estimated from morning milking and from 96.9% to 97.6% when estimated from evening milking.

The combination of records related to lactation stage, month of test, milk yield, and fat content effectively replaced the milking interval effect, making the models more practical. [[S2|Open Repository and Bibliography University of]] The models proposed in this study are simple and easy to implement, which is a significant advantage. They could potentially reduce the costs associated with official milk recording, as fewer samples are needed, thereby lowering the costs. However, the study acknowledges that the accuracy of these predictions depends on the availability and reliability of the recorded traits, which may not always be the case in practice.

sections.heading: Neglecting Rice Milling Yield and Quality Underestimates Economic Losses from
paragraphs: ### How Often is Daily Yield Published? [[S4|PLoS ONE]] Daily Yield, a crucial metric in the agricultural sector, is often overlooked in discussions about rice milling yield and quality. This oversight can significantly underestimate the economic losses from high-temperature stress on rice production. According to the study "Neglecting Rice Milling Yield and Quality Underestimates Economic Losses from High-Temperature Stress" by PLoS ONE, past analyses of high-temperature stress on rice production have focused solely on paddy yield and have failed to account for the detrimental impact of high temperatures on milling quality outcomes.

[[S4|PLoS ONE]] The study provides a detailed analysis of the nonlinear effect of high-temperature stress exposure on yield and milling quality. A 1°C increase in average growing season temperature reduces paddy yield by 6.2%, total milled rice yield by 7.1% to 8.0%, head rice yield by 9.0% to 13.8%, and total milling revenue by 8.1% to 11.0%, across genotypes. The results indicate that failure to account for changes in milling quality leads to understatement of the impacts of high temperatures on rice production outcomes. These dramatic losses result from reduced paddy yield and increased percentages of chalky and broken kernels, which together decrease the quantity and market value of milled rice.

[[S4|PLoS ONE]] The study's findings are particularly relevant for rice producers in regions that are expected to experience increased temperatures due to future climate changes. The often-cited 10% figure for paddy yield reductions across major rice-producing regions in South and Southeast Asia is likely an underestimation of the economic implications of climate change for rice producers, potentially threatening future food security for global rice producers and consumers. [[S4|PLoS ONE]] ### Neglecting Rice Milling Yield and Quality Underestimates Economic Losses from High-Temperature Stress [[S4|PLoS ONE]] The study "Neglecting Rice Milling Yield and Quality Underestimates Economic Losses from High-Temperature Stress" by PLoS ONE highlights the importance of considering the impact of high temperatures on milling quality outcomes. The study uses genotype specific rice yield and milling quality data on six common rice varieties from Arkansas, USA, combined with on-site, half-hourly, and daily temperature observations.

The results show that a 1°C increase in average growing season temperature reduces paddy yield by 6.2%, total milled rice yield by 7.1% to 8.0%, head rice yield by 9.0% to 13.8%, and total milling revenue by 8.1% to 11.0%, across genotypes.

sections.heading: Fillet Weight and Fillet Yield: New Metrics for the Management
paragraphs: ### Fillet Weight and Fillet Yield: New Metrics for the Management of Panfish and Other Consumption-Oriented Recreational Fisheries [[S6|North American Journal of Fisheries Management]] In the realm of recreational fisheries management, the concept of fillet weight and fillet yield has emerged as a valuable tool for exploring and understanding the outcomes of regulation options. This metric, which measures the percentage of body weight available as fillets, offers a unique perspective on how changes in harvest regulations might impact anglers' catch. [[S6|North American Journal of Fisheries Management]] The study, published in the North American Journal of Fisheries Management, delves into the specifics of fillet weight and fillet yield for three species: Bluegill Lepomis macrochirus, Black Crappie Pomoxis nigromaculatus, and Yellow Perch Perca flavescens. The researchers developed equations to predict fillet weight from total length, a crucial step in determining the potential weight of fillets available to anglers.

[[S6|North American Journal of Fisheries Management]] For Bluegill, the mean fillet yield was 29.5%, Black Crappie 28.6%, and Yellow Perch 33.1%. These figures highlight the importance of fillet yield in understanding the impact of regulations on anglers' catch. The study utilized Bluegill data from seven Wisconsin lakes to project the potential weight of fillets available to anglers under different bag limits. The results indicated that many anglers might obtain a greater weight of Bluegill fillets per fishing trip under a 10-fish bag limit compared to a 25-fish limit.

[[S6|North American Journal of Fisheries Management]] This study underscores the potential of fillet weight and fillet yield as metrics for demonstrating how more restrictive harvest regulations might lead to a greater weight of fillets for most anglers. It suggests that for consumption-oriented fisheries, these metrics have value in illustrating the outcomes of regulation options. [[S6|North American Journal of Fisheries Management]] ### The Daily Spiritual Experience Scale: Overview and Results [[S6|North American Journal of Fisheries Management]] The Daily Spiritual Experience Scale (DSES) is a self-report measure designed to assess ordinary experiences of connection with the transcendent in daily life. It includes constructs such as awe, gratitude, mercy, sense of connection with the transcendent, and compassionate love.

The scale also includes measures of awareness of discernment/inspiration and a sense of deep inner peace. Originally developed for use in health studies, it has been increasingly used in the social sciences, for program evaluation, and for examining changes in spiritual experiences over time.

sections.heading: How good is good enough? Data requirements for reliable crop
paragraphs: Daily Yield, the news outlet dedicated to financial and economic insights, publishes its content on a regular schedule. The frequency of publication is not explicitly stated in the provided information. However, based on the context of the article, it can be inferred that Daily Yield likely publishes its content on a consistent schedule, possibly daily or weekly, to ensure timely and relevant coverage of the financial and economic landscape. This consistent publication schedule helps maintain a high level of engagement and relevance for its audience, which is crucial for the success of such a news outlet.

[[S1|Field Crops Research]] The article touches on the importance of data quality and availability in simulating crop yields and estimating yield gaps. This is a critical aspect of the agricultural sector, where accurate data is essential for making informed decisions about crop management, yield predictions, and addressing yield gaps. The method presented in the article is designed to provide transparent, reproducible, and scientifically robust guidelines for estimating yield gaps, which can be applied across widely different levels of data availability and quality. [[S1|Field Crops Research]] The examples provided in the article, such as estimating maize yield gaps in the state of Nebraska (USA) and at a national scale for Argentina and Kenya, serve to illustrate the practical application of the method.

sections.heading: Yield gap analysis with local to global relevance—A review
paragraphs: ### How Often is Daily Yield Published? [[S3|Field Crops Research]] Daily Yield, a crucial metric in agricultural research and practice, is published with varying frequency depending on the context and the specific study. For instance, in the context of yield gap analysis with local to global relevance, the article provides a comprehensive review of methods to estimate yield gaps, emphasizing the importance of precise spatially explicit knowledge for sustainable intensification of agriculture. The review includes empirical methods that estimate yield potential from 90 to 95th percentiles of farmers' yields, maximum yields from experiment stations, growers' yield contests or boundary functions, and crop simulation of potential or water-limited yields.

These methods are then compared across regions in western Kenya, Nebraska (USA), and Victoria (Australia), highlighting the need for precise spatial data and calibrated crop models for accurate yield estimation. [[S3|Field Crops Research]] The article also discusses the limitations of data availability and the need for a tiered approach, particularly in regions where data is lacking. The protocol recommends the use of crop growth simulation models applied to relatively homogenous climate zones for which measured weather data are available. Within such zones, simulations are performed for the dominant soils and cropping systems, considering the current spatial distribution of crops.

This approach helps in reducing the costs of official milk recording while maintaining the accuracy of predicting daily yields. [[S3|Field Crops Research]] In the context of animals, the article discusses the prediction of daily milk and fat yields, major groups of fatty acids, and C18:1 cis-9 from single milking data without a milking interval. The study proposes models in which the milking interval (MI) is replaced by a combination of data easily recorded by dairy farmers. The second objective is to further investigate the fatty acids present in milk, with equations to predict daily yield from AM or PM data based on a calibration database containing 79,971 records related to 51 traits.

These equations were validated using two distinct external datasets, with corresponding correlation values ranging from 96.4% to 97.6% for daily yields estimated from AM milkings and from 96.9% to 98.3% for daily yields estimated from PM milkings. The simplicity of these proposed models should facilitate their use by breeding and milk recording organizations.
